parent_patents_act_sec_10.title: Patents Act 1970 - Section 10(4)(d)(ii): Mandatory Disclosure of Biological Source and Origin
parent_patents_act_sec_10.full_text:
The Patents Act, 1970 - Section 10: Contents of specifications.
(4) Every complete specification shall—
(d) be accompanied by an abstract to provide technical information on the invention:
Provided that—
(ii) if the applicant mentions a biological material in the specification which may not be available to the public or if biological material from India is used in the invention, the applicant must disclose the source and geographical origin of the biological material in the specification.
Failure to disclose or wrongly mentioning the source and geographical origin of the Indian biological resource is a statutory ground for pre-grant opposition under Section 25(1)(j), post-grant opposition under Section 25(2)(j), and revocation of the patent under Section 64(1)(p).

parent_patents_act_sec_25.title: Patents Act 1970 - Section 25: Opposition to Grant of Patent on Traditional Knowledge Grounds
parent_patents_act_sec_25.full_text:
The Patents Act, 1970 - Section 25: Opposition to the patent.
(1) Where an application for a patent has been published but a patent has not been granted, any person may, in writing, represent by way of opposition to the Controller on the grounds:
(k) that the complete specification does not disclose or wrongly mentions the source or geographical origin of biological material used for the invention;
(l) that the invention so far as claimed in any claim of the complete specification was anticipated having regard to the knowledge, oral or otherwise, available within any local or indigenous community in India or elsewhere (traditional knowledge prior art).
(2) At any time after the grant of patent but before the expiry of a period of one year from the date of publication of grant of patent, any person interested may give notice of opposition to the Controller on the grounds of lack of novelty, obviousness, Section 3 exclusions, non-disclosure of biological origin, or traditional knowledge anticipation.

parent_bda_sec_3.title: Biological Diversity Act 2002 - Section 3: Approval of NBA for Non-Indian Entities
parent_bda_sec_3.full_text:
The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 - Section 3: Certain persons not to undertake Biodiversity related activities without approval of National Biodiversity Authority.
(1) No person who is not a citizen of India, or a citizen of India who is non-resident (NRI), or a body corporate, association or organization not incorporated or registered in India, or incorporated or registered in India under any law for the time being in force which has any non-Indian participation in its share capital or management, shall, without the previous approval of the National Biodiversity Authority, obtain any biological resource occurring in India or knowledge associated thereto for research or for commercial utilization or for bio-survey and bio-utilization.
Foreign entities, foreign-owned or foreign-controlled companies, and NRIs must apply for prior approval through Form I of the NBA Regulations before accessing any Indian medicinal herbs, extracts, or Ayurvedic bio-resources.

parent_bda_sec_6.title: Biological Diversity Act 2002 - Section 6: Prior NBA Approval (Form III) for Patent Applications
parent_bda_sec_6.full_text:
The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 - Section 6: Application for intellectual property rights not to be made without approval of National Biodiversity Authority.
(1) No person shall apply for any intellectual property right, by whatever name called, in or outside India for any invention based on any research or information on a biological resource obtained from India without obtaining the previous approval of the National Biodiversity Authority before grant of such intellectual property right:
Provided that in case of making an application for patents, permission of the National Biodiversity Authority may be obtained after making the application but before the grant of the patent by the patent office.
(2) The National Biodiversity Authority while granting approval under this section may impose benefit sharing fee or royalty or conditions incurring sharing of financial benefits arising out of the commercial utilization of such rights (typically 1% to 3% of the ex-factory sale price or 0.1% to 0.5% of turnover).
Mandatory NBA Form III application must be submitted and approved before the Indian Patent Office issues the patent grant.

parent_bda_sec_7.title: Biological Diversity Act 2002 - Section 7: Prior Intimation to State Biodiversity Board (SBB)
parent_bda_sec_7.full_text:
The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 - Section 7: Prior intimation to State Biodiversity Board for obtaining biological resource for certain purposes.
No person who is a citizen of India or a body corporate, association or organisation which is registered in India shall obtain any biological resource for commercial utilisation, or bio-survey and bio-utilisation for commercial utilisation except after giving prior intimation to the State Biodiversity Board concerned:
Provided that the provisions of this section shall not apply to the local people and communities of the area, including growers and cultivators of biodiversity, and vaids and hakims, who have been practicing indigenous medicine.
Indian companies and domestic AYUSH manufacturers must provide prior intimation to the concerned SBB (Form I-A) and comply with state ABS benefit sharing requirements.

parent_bda_sec_40.title: Biological Diversity Act 2002 - Section 40: Normally Traded Commodities (NTC) Exemption
parent_bda_sec_40.full_text:
The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 - Section 40: Power of Central Government to exempt certain biological resources.
Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, the Central Government may, in consultation with the National Biodiversity Authority, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare that the provisions of this Act shall not apply to any items, including biological resources normally traded as commodities, or to items derived from sources of agriculture, horticulture, or conventional cultivation.
The Section 40 NTC notification exempts over 400 listed biological resources (such as black pepper, ginger, garlic, clove, and turmeric) from the provisions of the Biological Diversity Act when traded purely as agricultural commodities for consumption, but NOT when exported or accessed as genetic material or raw extracts for proprietary IPR/patents.

parent_drugs_cosmetics_act_1940.title: Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 & First Schedule: Ayurvedic Formulation Categorization
parent_drugs_cosmetics_act_1940.full_text:
Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 - Section 3(a) & The First Schedule.
Section 3(a) defines 'Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani (ASU) drug' as including all medicines intended for internal or external use for or in the diagnosis, treatment, mitigation or prevention of disease or disorder in human beings or animals, and manufactured exclusively in accordance with the formulae described in the authoritative books of Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani systems of medicine, specified in the First Schedule.
The First Schedule lists authoritative classical treatises including Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, Ashtanga Hridaya, Sarngadhara Samhita, Bhavaprakasha, Ayurvedic Formulary of India (AFI), and Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API).
Under Drugs and Cosmetics Rules (Rule 158B):
- Classical ASU formulations manufactured strictly according to First Schedule texts are exempt from safety and clinical trial requirements under Rule 158B(I).
- Patent or Proprietary ASU Medicines (non-classical novel extractions or modern combinations) require submission of safety, stability, and clinical efficacy data under Rule 158B(II).

parent_ipindia_patent_guidelines_tk.title: IP India Guidelines for Patent Applications: Traditional Knowledge & Biological Material
parent_ipindia_patent_guidelines_tk.full_text:
Office of the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (IP India) - Guidelines for Examination of Patent Applications related to Traditional Knowledge and Biological Material.
The Patent Office applies strict guiding principles for assessing patentability under Section 3(p), Section 3(d), and Section 3(e):
1. Guiding Principle 1: If the combination of herbs or ingredients is disclosed in classical texts or TKDL prior art, it is presumed to be non-novel.
2. Guiding Principle 2: Mere aggregation of known medicinal properties does not satisfy the inventive step requirement. A synergistic combination showing unexpected therapeutic effect (demonstrated by isobolograms, combination indices CI < 1, or statistical animal models) must be conclusively proven.
3. Guiding Principle 3: Extraction of an active fraction from a known Ayurvedic plant using routine extraction solvents (water, ethanol) is deemed obvious unless an unexpected new chemical entity or delivery mode is created.
4. Guiding Principle 4: Disclosure of biological source under Section 10(4)(d)(ii) is mandatory; examiner must raise an objection if source is missing.
5. Guiding Principle 5: The Patent Office shall not grant any patent without formal proof of NBA Form III approval whenever Indian bio-resources are claimed.

parent_ipindia_trademarks_class5.title: Trade Marks Manual Class 5 - Section 9: Exclusion of Generic Ayurvedic Herb Names
parent_ipindia_trademarks_class5.full_text:
Trade Marks Registry (IP India) - Examination of Trade Marks in Class 5 (Pharmaceutical and Herbal Formulations).
Section 9(1)(b) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 prohibits the registration of trade marks which consist exclusively of marks or indications which may serve in trade to designate the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, values, geographical origin, or time of production of goods.
Generic, classical, or common botanical names of Ayurvedic herbs (including but not limited to 'Ashwagandha', 'Triphala', 'Chyawanprash', 'Brahmi', 'Shatavari', 'Tulsi', 'Neem', 'Amla', 'Guggulu') are Publici Juris (belonging to the public). No individual or company can claim exclusive monopolistic trademark ownership over the generic name of a classical formulation or medicinal plant in Class 5. Trademark protection is permissible only for distinctive brand prefixes, inventive coined terms, or stylized distinctive device marks.

parent_ipindia_gi_guidelines.title: Geographical Indications Registry: Traditional Ayurvedic Heritage Protections
parent_ipindia_gi_guidelines.full_text:
Geographical Indications Registry (IP India) - Protection of Traditional and Indigenous Products.
Under the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, traditional Ayurvedic medicines, specialized medicinal rice varieties (such as Navara Rice), and localized traditional healing substances associated with specific geographical regions, traditional cultivation practices, or historical lineage can be protected as collective Geographical Indications.
GI registration protects registered proprietor collectives, farmers, and traditional cultivators against deceptive marketing and misappropriation, establishing community-based intellectual property distinct from individual private patents.

parent_nba_form_3_ipr.title: National Biodiversity Authority - Form III Application for Intellectual Property Rights (Patents)
parent_nba_form_3_ipr.full_text:
National Biodiversity Authority (NBA India) - Form III: Application for seeking prior approval of National Biodiversity Authority for applying for Intellectual Property Right.
Under Section 6 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 and Regulation 8 of the ABS Regulations, 2014:
1. Every applicant seeking a patent in India or overseas for an invention involving or based on biological resources or traditional knowledge obtained from India must submit Form III to the NBA along with the prescribed statutory fee (INR 500).
2. Timing of Approval: The applicant must file Form III and obtain formal NBA approval prior to the grant of the patent. The Indian Patent Office will hold grant proceedings in abeyance pending NBA clearance.
3. Benefit Sharing Obligations: NBA executes an Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) agreement with the patentee. Where the applicant commercializes the patent directly, benefit sharing is typically assessed between 0.2% and 1.0% of the annual ex-factory gross sales, or between 2% and 5% of licensing fees/royalties received from third-party assignees.

parent_nba_form_1_commercial.title: National Biodiversity Authority - Form I Application for Commercial Utilization
parent_nba_form_1_commercial.full_text:
National Biodiversity Authority (NBA India) - Form I: Application for access to biological resources and associated knowledge for commercial utilization.
Under Section 3 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 and Regulation 2 of the ABS Regulations, 2014:
Non-Indian individuals, NRIs, and foreign companies (including Indian entities with any non-resident shareholding or directors) must file Form I with the NBA prior to accessing, procuring, or utilizing Indian biological resources for commercial drug manufacturing, extract production, or commercial research.
Statutory application fee is INR 10,000. Benefit sharing is assessed at:
- 0.1% for annual gross ex-factory sale of product up to INR 1,00,00,000;
- 0.2% for annual sales between INR 1,00,00,001 and INR 3,00,00,000;
- 0.5% for annual sales exceeding INR 3,00,00,000.

parent_nba_bda_2023_amendment.title: Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act 2023: AYUSH Practitioner & Cultivated Herb Exemptions
parent_nba_bda_2023_amendment.full_text:
Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023 - Key Statutory Amendments and Decriminalization Provisions.
The 2023 Amendment to the Biological Diversity Act introduced pivotal modifications for the AYUSH and herbal industry:
1. AYUSH Practitioner Exemption: Registered AYUSH practitioners (vaids, hakims, siddha/sowa-rigpa practitioners) are explicitly exempted from giving prior intimation to State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs) for accessing biological resources to prepare traditional formulations in their customary healing practice.
2. Cultivated Medicinal Plants Exemption: Access to cultivated medicinal plants (duly registered under state agriculture/AYUSH portals) is exempted from commercial access restrictions, encouraging formal agro-farming of medicinal flora.
3. Indian Companies Clarification: Re-defines 'foreign entity' to exempt Indian-incorporated entities that do not qualify as foreign-controlled under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA).
4. Decriminalization: Replaces imprisonment with civil financial penalties adjudicated by designated adjudicating officers, removing criminal prosecution for unintentional administrative delays.

parent_nba_abs_guidelines.title: NBA Guidelines on Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) Regulations 2014 Schedule
parent_nba_abs_guidelines.full_text:
National Biodiversity Authority - Guidelines on Access to Biological Resources and Associated Knowledge and Benefits Sharing Regulations, 2014.
Notification G.S.R. 823(E).
Key Benefit Sharing Guidelines:
- Option 1 (Sales based): The buyer/manufacturer pays to the NBA/SBB an amount ranging from 0.1% to 0.5% of the annual gross ex-factory sale of product.
- Option 2 (Purchase price based): For traders and manufacturers purchasing raw biological resources, benefit sharing between 1.0% and 3.0% of the purchase price of the biological resource.
- Option 3 (High economic value biological resources): SBB/NBA may determine higher benefit sharing up to 5% for rare, endangered, or highly prioritized endemic botanical species.
Benefit sharing funds are remitted by NBA to Local Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs) to incentivize conservation and benefit tribal and forest cultivators.

parent_tkdl_public_scope.title: Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) - Public Purpose, Architecture & Scope
parent_tkdl_public_scope.full_text:
Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL - https://tkdl.res.in) - Public Purpose, Architecture and Scope.
The Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) is a pioneering Indian digital repository established as a joint initiative between the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) and the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
Public Mission and Scope:
1. Defensive Protection of Traditional Knowledge: TKDL breaks the language barrier that historically permitted biopiracy and wrongful patenting of traditional Indian medicine abroad. It translates traditional knowledge from ancient texts in Sanskrit, Hindi, Arabic, Persian, Urdu, and Tamil into five international languages: English, French, German, Japanese, and Spanish.
2. Comprehensive Textual Codification: TKDL contains over 4.5 lakh (450,000) formulations documented from authoritative classical treatises of Ayurveda (such as Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, Ashtanga Hridaya, Chakradatta, Sarngadhara Samhita, Bhaisajya Ratnavali, and AFI), Unani, Siddha, and Sowa-Rigpa.
3. Prior Art Grounding: Information in TKDL provides conclusive statutory prior art establishing that classical Ayurvedic formulations and single/polyherbal compositions are known to the public, barring patent novelty under Section 3(p) of the Patents Act 1970 and international patent criteria.

parent_tkdl_access_agreements.title: TKDL International Patent Office Access Agreements for Prior Art Search
parent_tkdl_access_agreements.full_text:
Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL - https://tkdl.res.in) - International Access Agreements.
Under bilateral Access and Non-Disclosure Agreements, the Government of India provides search access to the TKDL database exclusively to examiners at major international patent offices:
- European Patent Office (EPO)
- United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO)
- Japan Patent Office (JPO)
- United Kingdom Intellectual Property Office (UKIPO)
- Canadian Intellectual Property Office (CIPO)
- German Patent and Trade Mark Office (DPMA)
- Australian Patent Office (IP Australia)
Patent examiners consult TKDL under confidentiality terms to conduct prior art searches on patent applications claiming traditional Indian herbs or Ayurvedic formulations. Third-party commercial access is strictly restricted, and automated scraping or CAPTCHA circumvention is prohibited.

parent_tkdl_tkrc_classification.title: Traditional Knowledge Resource Classification (TKRC) System
parent_tkdl_tkrc_classification.full_text:
Traditional Knowledge Resource Classification (TKRC) System.
Developed by CSIR and Ministry of Ayush, the Traditional Knowledge Resource Classification (TKRC) maps ancient Ayurvedic, Unani, and Siddha medical concepts to the International Patent Classification (IPC) structure used by patent examiners worldwide.
TKRC structures classical knowledge into:
- Section A: Human Necessities (Sub-sections for Ayurveda AK01 to AK15).
- Precise indexing of plant scientific binomial nomenclature, classical Sanskrit names, medicinal parts used (roots, leaves, bark, fruits), extraction methods, dosage forms (Asava, Arishta, Churna, Vati, Taila, Bhasma), and therapeutic indications.
This systematic taxonomy enables instant cross-referencing between modern patent claims and ancient classical recipes.

parent_tkdl_defensive_outcomes.title: TKDL Defensive Protection Outcomes: Pre-Grant Oppositions & Patent Revocations
parent_tkdl_defensive_outcomes.full_text:
Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) - Defensive Protection Outcomes.
TKDL has achieved landmark global victories defending Indian traditional knowledge against misappropriation:
1. Over 250 international patent applications filed across the US, Europe, and Japan claiming therapeutic applications of Ashwagandha, Turmeric, Neem, Cumin, Pudina, and Triphala have been cancelled, withdrawn, or amended following third-party prior art submissions by the TKDL team.
2. Classical formulations (like Chyawanprash for immunomodulation, Triphala for digestive disorders, and Ashwagandha for stress) have been conclusively established as non-patentable public prior art worldwide.
3. Proof of novelty for Ayurvedic formulations requires going beyond TKDL classical prior art disclosures by proving non-obvious synergistic compositions, novel delivery liposomes/nanoparticles, or specific chemically modified fractions.

children.text: Section 3(p) of Patents Act 1970 excludes an invention which in effect is traditional knowledge or which is an aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditionally known component or components.
Under Section 3(p), combining known Ayurvedic medicinal plants without proving unexpected synergistic enhancement is non-patentable prior art.
Section 3(d) excludes the mere discovery of a new form of a known substance which does not result in enhancement of the known efficacy of that substance.
Section 3(e) excludes substances obtained by a mere admixture resulting only in the aggregation of the properties of the components thereof.
Patents for Ayurvedic herbal extracts require proof of synergistic interaction or novel delivery mechanism to overcome Section 3(p) and 3(e) exclusions.
Section 10(4)(d)(ii) of the Patents Act 1970 mandates that every patent specification using biological material from India must disclose its source and geographical origin.
Failure to disclose or wrongly mentioning the source or geographical origin of biological material in a patent specification triggers opposition under Section 25.
Under Section 64(1)(p), a patent may be revoked if the complete specification does not disclose or wrongly mentions the source and geographical origin of the biological material.
Section 25(1)(k) allows any person to file pre-grant opposition if the patent specification wrongly mentions or omits the source or geographical origin of Indian biological material.
Section 25(1)(l) provides statutory grounds for patent opposition if the claimed invention was anticipated by traditional knowledge available in local or indigenous communities.
Post-grant opposition under Section 25(2) can be filed within one year of grant based on traditional knowledge anticipation or non-compliance with biological source disclosures.
Section 3 of Biological Diversity Act 2002 prohibits non-Indian citizens, NRIs, and foreign-invested companies from obtaining Indian biological resources without prior approval of the NBA.
Entities with any non-Indian shareholding or foreign management must obtain NBA approval via Form I before accessing Indian medicinal herbs or bio-resources.
Section 3 covers access for commercial utilization, research, bio-survey, and bio-utilization of Indian botanical flora and fauna.
Section 6(1) of Biological Diversity Act 2002 requires mandatory NBA approval before the grant of a patent for any invention based on Indian biological resources.
Under Section 6, patent applicants can file their patent application first, but must secure NBA Form III approval before patent grant.
Section 6(2) empowers the NBA to determine benefit sharing obligations, requiring payment of royalties or sharing of financial gains from commercial utilization.
NBA Form III clearance is an absolute prerequisite for patent grant on any Ayurvedic formulation utilizing Indian botanical components.
Section 7 mandates that Indian citizens and domestic entities must give prior intimation to the State Biodiversity Board (SBB) before accessing biological resources for commercial utilization.
Under Section 7, traditional vaids, hakims, local communities, and registered cultivators of medicinal herbs are exempt from prior intimation when practicing indigenous medicine.
Commercial AYUSH drug manufacturers operating in India must file Form I-A with the relevant SBB and adhere to state ABS revenue-sharing rules.
Section 40 empowers the Central Government to exempt biological resources normally traded as commodities (NTC) from the provisions of the Biological Diversity Act.
Items listed in the Section 40 NTC Gazette notification are exempt from ABS regulations when traded strictly as agricultural commodities for consumption.
The Section 40 NTC exemption does not apply if the commodity is accessed as genetic material, patented, or used as proprietary biological research for filing IPR.
Section 3(a) of Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 defines Ayurvedic drugs as medicines manufactured in accordance with formulae described in First Schedule authoritative texts.
The First Schedule lists canonical Ayurvedic texts including Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, Ashtanga Hridaya, AFI, and API.
Under Rule 158B(I), classical Ayurvedic formulations conforming to First Schedule literature require no new clinical safety trials for manufacturing licensing.
Under Rule 158B(II), Patent or Proprietary Ayurvedic medicines require proof of safety, published literature, and stability data for drug license issuance.
IP India Guidelines specify that herbal combinations disclosed in classical Ayurvedic literature or TKDL are presumed non-patentable under Section 3(p).

Section 9(1)(b) of Trade Marks Act 1999 prohibits registration of generic, descriptive Ayurvedic herb names as exclusive trademarks in Class 5.
Common Ayurvedic names like Ashwagandha, Triphala, Brahmi, and Tulsi are publici juris and cannot be monopolized by any single manufacturer.

The Geographical Indications Act 1999 protects localized Ayurvedic formulations, therapeutic agricultural varieties (e.g. Navara rice), and regional traditional healing arts.
GI registration grants collective community protection, safeguarding traditional cultivator associations from commercial misappropriation.
Unlike individual patents, Geographical Indications protect perpetual heritage and cannot be commercialized as an exclusive private corporate monopoly.
NBA Form III is the mandatory statutory application required before patent grant for any invention utilizing Indian biological resources.
Under ABS Regulation 8, patent applicants must submit Form III to the NBA with the prescribed statutory fee before the patent office issues grant.

The Indian Patent Office will not seal or grant a patent specification until formal NBA Form III approval is placed on record.
NBA Form I must be filed by foreign entities, NRIs, and foreign-invested companies prior to accessing Indian bio-resources for commercial utilization.
Form I approval involves progressive benefit sharing rates from 0.1% to 0.5% of ex-factory gross annual sales.
Commercial manufacture of herbal products by foreign-invested enterprises without Form I approval constitutes a cognizable offense under the BD Act.
The 2023 Biological Diversity Amendment explicitly exempts registered AYUSH medical practitioners from prior SBB intimation for customary traditional medicine practice.
Cultivated medicinal plants registered under agricultural systems are granted exemptions from certain ABS access restrictions under the 2023 Amendment.
The 2023 Amendment decriminalized procedural non-compliance, replacing criminal penalties with civil adjudicatory penalties under the BD Act.
Under ABS Regulations 2014, manufacturers can elect benefit sharing of 0.1% to 0.5% of annual gross ex-factory sales or 1.0% to 3.0% of raw material purchase price.
